title: The bridge photo
claim: URGENT!!! Riverbend Bridge has COLLAPSED after last night's floods. Many people trapped. Share before they delete this!!
claimSource: Forwarded in a WhatsApp group, then spotted on three social accounts. A rival outlet has just shared it.
briefing: It is late afternoon. A photo of a collapsed bridge is spreading fast and your next news slot is at 18:00. You cannot check everything. Choose what to check, work out what each result really proves, then decide what goes out.

checks.label: Reverse image search
checks.desc: Run the photo through reverse image search to find where else it has appeared.
checks.hint: Recycled photos are the most common trick, and this check is quick.
checks.result: The same picture appears on a foreign news site and a photo library, dated 2021. It was captioned as flooding in another country.
checks.why: A dated original that predates the claim is strong, checkable evidence that the photo is recycled.

checks.label: Call the road authority press office
checks.desc: Ask the body responsible for the bridge whether it has collapsed, and ask for a named, on-the-record answer.
checks.hint: Go to the people responsible, and get the answer attributed to a named person.
checks.result: A named officer says there is no collapse. Engineers inspected the bridge this morning and it is open, with one lane restricted because of high water.
checks.why: The body responsible answered directly on the exact claim and will stand behind it. It is also your right of reply.

checks.label: Geolocate the photo
checks.desc: Compare signs, traffic, terrain and the riverbank in the photo with the real bridge.
checks.hint: Look for details in the picture that you can test against the real place.
checks.result: Road signs are in a language not used in this district, traffic keeps to the opposite side of the road, and the riverbank does not match the real bridge.
checks.why: Several independent details in the image contradict the claimed location, which is strong evidence.

checks.label: Check the first account that posted it
checks.desc: Look at when the account was created, who follows it and what it usually posts.
checks.hint: A suspicious account is a flag, not a verdict.
checks.result: The account was created three days ago, has 40 followers and only posts forwarded images.
checks.why: A brand-new account is a warning sign, but real events are also posted by new accounts. It points somewhere without proving anything.

checks.label: Search other outlets, police and wires
checks.desc: See whether anyone credible has reported a collapse.
checks.hint: No reports is a pointer, not proof. A story can break before anyone writes it up.
checks.result: No other outlet, police statement or wire report mentions a collapse.
checks.why: Silence from others fits a false claim, but it also fits a very new real event. Treat it as supporting, not conclusive.

checks.label: Phone a resident near the bridge
checks.desc: Ask someone on the ground what they can see right now.
checks.hint: One witness is useful but only one source.
checks.result: A resident says the river is high and people are nervous, but the bridge is standing.
checks.why: A single eyewitness helps, but one source who may also have heard the rumour is not enough on its own.

checks.label: Read the photo's metadata
checks.desc: Look for camera data, a date or GPS coordinates inside the image file.
checks.hint: Messaging apps often strip this data.
checks.result: The file has no camera data, date or location. The messaging app stripped it all.
checks.why: Missing metadata proves nothing either way. Most shared images lose it, so this check rarely helps with forwards.

checks.label: Message the original poster for their source
checks.desc: Ask where they got the photo and whether they took it.
checks.hint: Good practice, but it can eat your clock. Do it alongside other checks, not instead of them.
checks.result: No reply before your deadline. You spent the time waiting.
checks.why: Contacting the source is worth doing, but you cannot count on a reply under deadline. Send the message and keep working.

reflect.title: Check yourself
reflect.prompt: The photo is alarming. A rival has just shared it, and someone on your team says “we can’t be last on this.” What do you do?

options.label: Go with the crowd: if everyone has it, it must be real.
options.explain: Popularity is not verification. Many people sharing a photo often means one false post copied many times.

options.label: Trust my gut: it looks real to me.
options.explain: A convincing look is exactly what good fakes and recycled photos have. Gut feeling is a reason to check, not a reason to publish.

options.label: Notice the pressure and my own reaction, and decide on evidence, not on being first.
options.explain: Naming the pressure and the emotion before deciding is the habit that stops you amplifying a falsehood.

options.label: Ask a colleague to challenge my assumptions before I decide.
options.explain: A second pair of eyes catches bias well. It scores slightly lower here only because the clock leaves little time for it.

create.title: Write the line
create.prompt: What do you put out? Choose the wording that fits what you actually know.

options.label: BREAKING: Bridge collapses in flooding. Pictures from social media show the damage.
options.explain: This amplifies an unverified claim and spreads the photo even further.

options.label: We are aware of an image circulating and are checking it with the authorities.
options.explain: A holding line is reasonable while evidence is thin. Once you hold strong evidence it undersells what you know.

options.label: No collapse: the viral bridge photo is from a 2021 flood abroad, and the road authority says the bridge is open.
options.explain: A clear correction that names the evidence and the authority is the strongest line, but only if you really hold that evidence.

options.label: Say nothing. It is just a rumour.
options.explain: The rumour is already spreading and people may act on it. Silence leaves the false version unchallenged.

act.title: Decide and act
act.prompt: It is nearly 18:00. What do you do?

options.label: Run the photo as breaking news.
options.explain: Publishing an unverified image under your name puts your credibility behind it.

options.label: Hold: no item this slot, and keep verifying for the next one.
options.explain: Holding is the right call when evidence is thin. With strong evidence in hand, holding wastes the chance to correct the record.

options.label: Publish a correction with the authority’s named comment, and explain how people can check images like this.
options.explain: Publishing the correction, with the right of reply included, serves the audience, provided your evidence is solid.

options.label: Forward the photo to colleagues and ask what they think.
options.explain: That spreads the unverified photo further without moving you toward a decision.

tells: The photo arrived with no original source, date or location.
The message used urgent, emotional wording and begged to be shared before it was “deleted”.
The first account to post it was brand new and only forwarded images.
A rival sharing it felt like pressure to follow, but that is not evidence.
Details in the picture (signs, traffic side, riverbank) did not match the place.

mediumNotes.print: Whatever you decide runs on tomorrow’s front page and the website.
mediumNotes.tv: Whatever you decide goes into the 18:00 TV bulletin.
mediumNotes.radio: Whatever you decide is read out in the 18:00 radio news.
mediumNotes.online: Whatever you decide is posted on the website and social accounts.
